unit: per job: one knock sensor replaced, on every example. On the two four-cylinder examples the engine's single sensor is bolted to the outside of the block. finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), each for ONE sensor with no diagnosis: economy 2016 Hyundai Elantra 2.0L about $150-$218 (0.9-1.0 hr); midsize 2017 Hyundai Tucson 2.0L about $162-$250 (1.0-1.2 hr); truck 2002 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 5.3L about $246-$406 (1.5-1.7 hr); luxury 2002 GMC Yukon Denali 6.0L about $246-$406 (1.5-1.7 hr). These sit well below the benchmarks (RepairPal $417-$589, Instant Car Fix $250-$550, J.D. Power $200-$800) and inside or near FIXD's $100-$400. Three things explain the gap. Every labor figure here is a manufacturer warranty time, which is the low end of what a shop bills: RepairPal carries $291-$427 in labor, about 1.8-3.6 hours at this rate, against our 0.9-1.7. Diagnosis is not in our totals and is almost always charged for this repair. And our low parts figures are genuine sensors at online discount prices ($42 and $66), where RepairPal's parts run $126-$161; on a V8 many shops also replace both sensors and the harness while the intake manifold is off, which this one-sensor job does not include (two genuine sensors are $131.20 online to $267.64 at list). How solid the labor times are: all eight range ends are manufacturer-stated times printed with a unit. Six are for the example vehicle (Hyundai TSB 26-01-033H for the Elantra and Tucson; GM bulletin 02-06-04-023 for the Silverado and Yukon Denali, read on an owners' site that reproduces it, not on a government or GM page). The economy and midsize high ends are the same Hyundai bulletin's times for a related vehicle, not the example. The two V8 times are for the rear sensor only; no stated time for the pair was found. Weak points: the luxury class rests on a 2002 GMC Yukon Denali, a luxury-trim truck-based SUV that shares the truck's engine layout and sensor, because no luxury-brand car had a stated time; a Lexus, Acura, BMW or other V6 or V8 with the sensors buried under the intake manifold can take much longer than 1.7 hours, and this file does not cover that. Both V8 examples are more than twenty years old. No aftermarket sensor price was usable as a low end because none of the retailer pages loaded states that the part is new; aftermarket sensors were listed at $27-$42 and would lower the totals.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (a knock sensor code can come from wiring, a connector or an engine fault, so the sensor is usually tested first), shop supplies and sales tax. Where the sensors sit under the intake manifold, expect intake manifold gaskets, the second sensor and the sensor wiring harness to be quoted at the same time, and sometimes coolant if the manifold carries it. An engine computer software update or a wiring repair is a separate charge when that is the real cause.
